review:
So, this game was made to empty the wallets of nostalgic 90's kids.

-> I am a 90's kid.
-> You know I'm gonna call this a masterpiece. Full stop.

If you've ever played any of the Naruto Storm games by Cyberconnect2 you are gonna find the combat in this game very familiar, the simple B button smash combos and fast dashes still remain and, when powered up, super attacks trigger cutscenes too. So overall a familiar feel to the combat, but in general Kakarot is its own beast.

Definitely the best thing about it is the amazing attention to detail from both manga and anime, I'll name a few of them:

-Power levels rise along with the story progression and are accurate in every event of the anime.
-Transforming strenghtens Saiyans ridiculously and makes other characters useless, just like in the anime.
-Stuffing your face with food before a battle is OP, just like in the anime.
-You go faster by flying. But you still use Nimbus. Because you know it's fun. Just like in the anime.
-You can race cars and ask Bulma for parts in her workshop, just like in the anime.
-Yes, you can properly collect Dragon Balls and spam Shenron wishes, just like in the anime.
-Korin gives you free Senzu beans overtime. Yes they are OP as they should, just like in the anime.
-The end game Super Spirit Bomb is so huge it's rendered out of the frame, just like in the anime.
-The cutscenes are... you know it. Just like the anime.

I could go on and on about every tiny detail there is, only noticed if you are a fan and care to look deeper, but it would be a long post. Hopefully these few things I mentioned are enough to make you buy the game and get immersed in what I think it's the best DBZ universe experience ever made. Go feed your inner kid some happiness, and it starts with that opening.

Not a fighting game.

Don't compare it to Tenkaichi or Xenoverse, because it's not even the same genre. It's an RPG with a semi-open world and some pretty neat but kinda simple combat once you get to grips with it. It's not ground breaking, and it's not Tenkaichi 4, so folks can just cool off.

But what it IS, is a really, REALLY enjoyable trip through the DBZ story, told better than ever before (in game format, anyways). It's rich, and deep, and pretty as all hell, and I love it for what it is.

At least, so far anyways. I'm about 3.5 hours in right now and I'd be playing more if I didn't have work in the morning. If I play more and decide that it's actually not that great, I'll update my review to reflect that, but as of right now these are my feelings. I saw a bunch of reviews compairing it to titles like Xenoverse 2, and decided to throw a counter arguement in there.

This is the essential canon DBZ experience you dreamed about when you were watching DBZ on Toonami in 1999.
It is canon to the manga, meaning it is like playing Dragon Ball Z Kai as an AARPG.
Here's how you should play the game:
- Watch for and do all blue ! quests as soon as they appear, or you will miss them. (But you can use the time machine later)
- Don't waste your time on collecting/exploring/grinding.
- Don't bother grinding at all. Just do the story.
- Visit Beerus at the beginning of the game.
- Visit Beerus to level up.
- The main story ends around 75. The main training ends at 100. 
- Visit Beerus to grind from 100 to 250.
- The vehicles are a completely optional side game and have no impact on anything whatsoever.
- Use Vegeta's big bang attack.
Picking apples and mining diamonds while Gohan is kidnapped and there is not an ounce of remorse in my body

I've been playing this game non-stop since its release (logged 80 hours so far), just finished the game (beat Kid Buu) and here are my thoughts.

Pros:
- Gameplay is engaging enough to keep an interest.
- Graphics are fresh and Unreal Engine does a great job at re-creating the anime.
- The storytelling is very accurate, and makes the player feel as if they are living through the anime.
- Lots of content.

Cons:
- Whilst gameplay is engaging, it can get repetitive quickly.
- There are numerous things to do, however, they can feel arduous to do as most side-quests are either killing things or fetching items.

Overall, I think the game is great and would definitely recommend it to other people! It's definitely the best Dragon Ball game I've played, and has been the game I've been waiting over 20 years for. :)

[h1]A true love letter for fans of DBZ [/h1]

When I was a kid and super into DBZ, this is the game I always wanted and imagined, but we never quite got. I would have played this non-stop for years if it came out in 2005 or so.

[u][b]The good:[/b][/u]
[list][*] Retells the four major sagas of Dragon Ball Z (Saiyans, Frieza, Cell, Buu) very faithfully, respects the source material, and is overall just a very authentic DBZ experience.
[*] Voice actors do a great job.
[*] The open world is fun to traverse and explore. It's not super densely packed, but this kind of works here because you can fly at lightspeed in freeroam.
[*] Lots of overlapping economies give a good reason to collect and hunt for materials.
[*] Collecting the Dragon Balls was made into a worthwhile open-world chase, as you can wish for money and rare items.[/list]

[u][b]The bad:[/b][/u]
[list][*] The combat is overly simplistic, button-mashy, and far too easy. There is no nuance or finesse to the combat.
[*] Combat can also be frustrating on the basis that control is wrestled away from the player a little too often for over the top enemy attack animations - This gets worse the further into the game you get.
[*] Staying faithful to the source material also means eyeroll-to-infinity dialogue that stretches far too long. I knew this was coming because it's DBZ, but... seriously, yikes
[*] Some major plot points are outright missing or glossed over (ie. about half of the Android plotline before Cell is replaced entirely by about two lines of text).[/list]


[u][b]The verdict:[/b][/u]

[b]Pick this up on sale, don't pay full price.[/b]

If you are, or were ever, a fan of Dragon Ball Z, I can definitely recommend this game - There is definitely something here that will make you smile. I haven't watched the anime since it originally aired, and I really enjoyed getting to relive the experience here.
Despite a lot of the individual components of the game honestly not being too great (such as the combat), this game really is greater than the sum of its parts, but I think it needs the nostalgia to make it work.
That being said, if you're not already a DBZ fan going in, there's a very real chance you won't enjoy this game all too much. If this is you, it might be worth reading some other reviews and watching some gameplay to help decide whether you want to buy this.

[h1] Honest Kakarot Complete Review [/h1]

This review is to help you deciding whether you are going to buy the game or not. Please be aware that part of this review can or not include spoilers but I feel every detail should be considered. I have completed 100% of the game.

Dragon Ball Z: Kakarot is an open world RPG game where you can explore most of Earth while using most of characters. Exploring experience is decent, with high quality visuals and details. Levelling system is acceptable, but it for sure is grindy. 
While travelling around, you can fight some enemies that give you EXP and Orbs which is most of you need to level up. There is no PVE mode like Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2 and there is no training mode. The "training" mode is only used to get more super attacks for your characters, and those can be very challenging if you do not meet level requirements. 
Story line/Main missions are VERY good, no questioning, If you are a Dragon Ball fan you will be very proud of this game, I almost felt like watching the Dragon Ball movie, so Unreal Engine 5 is a must from now on.

Overall Dragon Ball: Kakarot does offer a great experience, it is a game to be played patiently, to enjoy the whole experience of Dragon Ball. If you like to rush, then you will miss most of the precious details. There are some positive and negative aspects of the game that will be mentioned before I conclude this review, and also some recommendations on what to do.

Positive aspects:

[list]
[*]Amazing graphics.
[*]Fun combat.
[*]Fidelity to Anime/Manga story.
[*]Very good for people that have NEVER seen or played Dragon Ball before.
[*]LOTS of missions and places to explore.
[*]Intuitive menu, simple and straight to the point. 
[*]Good Skill Tree and Character menu, self explanatory.
[*]I LOVED transformations(except for one), combat animations 10/10 , very satisfying
[/list]

Negative aspects:
[list]
[*]If you do NOT like a lot of dialogue, this game sometimes can be painful, but it is meant to be that way. Also there are some missions that will require you to keep going back and forth to places instead of just showing a cut scene straight to the end of the mission(nothing you can do about, that's how the game goes as well).

[*]if you decide to skip SIDE missions, you will have to RE-DO some chapters as a whole and there is NO WAY to save progress with [spoiler] the time machine[/spoiler], so if anything happens you will lose progress and you will have to start over.

[*]Very reliant in character levelling. There is simply no way you are going to beat an enemy that easily without healing. So yes, it is going to be VERY hard sometimes to get new super attacks in training and EVEN if you try very hard, it might not work.

[*]BANDAI decided to add voice lines to characters so EVERY SINGLE TIME you collect an item or food it is going to spam that line. No, there is nothing you can do unless you go to setting and disable some of the sound(Which I would not recommend, sound is very important for experience).

[*]Dragon Balls COULD have more options/potential to wishes. MOST of wishes are lame(seriously), I would say 70%-80% lead to side quests which WILL give you some soul emblems, but that's not something CRUCIAL The rest of the options will only give you Z ORBS(easily collected fighting), Zeni/Money (Just sell some items I guess?) or Rare Items(This one is MAYBE the best wish, because it is boring sometimes to go all over the place and collect VERY specific items).

[*]Side quests could be more elaborated, this side quest system reminded me of Assassins Creed Odyssey where most of the time it's about collecting, HOWEVER it is compensated by extra story details for the characters, which I liked.

[*][spoiler] Vegito Fusion is BAD. You can only transform to Super Saiyan, it is weaker compared to Super Saiyan Blue and of course, you CANNOT transform to Vegito Blue without Mods. [/spoiler]
[/list]

Some tips:
[list]
[*] Please take your time to complete every chapter and respective side quests, trust me it is going to be hard to go back and complete it all with[spoiler] the time machine[/spoiler]

[*] Try keeping up with story line level so it is not too hard, not required but you should consider it. 

[*]As soon as you get Dragon Balls, start making wishes, anything. Try knocking out reviving some characters first! You will thank me later.

[*] Take your time to explore and gather as many resources as you can so you save time on side quests!

[*]Get as many recipes as you can and abuse from extra stats, do not think you won't need it. It is easy as going to a campfire or going to Chichi to prepare some food.

[*]Always check Skill tree so you have everything max level.


[b] Do I recommend Dragon Ball: Kakarot? [/b]

Yes, but wait for a good sale so you can get ALL of the DLC's. I got mine for $30.
It can also get even better with mods, but trying completing the game first as it is then you mess up with it later on. 
You will have a ton of fun. trust me. 

I hope this helps,

DRAGON BALL Z: KAKAROT is an expansive action RPG built around the idea of experiencing the Dragon Ball Z saga rather than simply fighting through its most famous battles. Developed by CyberConnect2 Co. Ltd. and published by Bandai Namco Entertainment Inc., the game combines cinematic combat, exploration, character progression, side quests, training, resource gathering, cooking, fishing, and interactions with familiar characters. Its strongest quality is the way these systems work together to create the feeling of participating in the everyday lives and extraordinary adventures of the Z Fighters.

The main story follows Goku and his allies through many of the defining conflicts of Dragon Ball Z. Instead of rushing from one opponent to another, the adventure spends considerable time on events between major battles. Players can explore different regions, interact with supporting characters, complete optional stories, train, gather ingredients, and prepare for upcoming confrontations. This structure gives the narrative more breathing room and helps distinguish the game from traditional Dragon Ball fighting titles. Fans already know where most of the story is heading, but actually controlling the characters throughout these events gives familiar material an entertaining interactive dimension.

Combat emphasizes accessibility and spectacle. Characters can freely move and fly around large three-dimensional battlefields while combining melee attacks, Ki blasts, evasive maneuvers, transformations, special techniques, and support abilities. Signature attacks are appropriately dramatic, with powerful visual effects and energetic camera work making important confrontations resemble playable anime sequences. The system is relatively easy to understand, allowing newcomers to perform impressive attacks without learning complicated fighting-game inputs. Character upgrades and increasingly demanding enemies provide additional depth, although the basic combat rhythm can become repetitive after many hours.

Progression incorporates several traditional RPG ideas. Characters gain experience, increase their attributes, unlock skills, improve special attacks, and obtain new abilities as the story advances. Training provides opportunities to strengthen combat capabilities, while food can offer useful bonuses. The Community Board system uses Soul Emblems associated with characters from the series and rewards thoughtful placement with different benefits. It is a creative way of turning relationships between characters into a progression mechanic, although players interested mainly in the story may find some of its optimization unnecessarily elaborate.

Exploration provides an enjoyable contrast to the constant destruction of the major battles. Players can fly across broad environments containing settlements, wilderness areas, resources, enemies, collectibles, fishing locations, and optional activities. Simply taking flight and traveling through recognizable Dragon Ball landscapes is satisfying, particularly during the earlier hours. Fishing, hunting, gathering ingredients, preparing meals, collecting items, and completing side stories help portray the characters as people who have lives beyond saving the world.

The environments are attractive and appropriately colorful, but their open structure is not consistently filled with meaningful activities. Collecting scattered objects eventually becomes routine, while encounters with weaker enemies can interrupt exploration more often than necessary. Side quests are similarly uneven. The better ones provide amusing conversations, appearances from recognizable characters, or additional context for the world, whereas simpler missions rely on basic collection or combat objectives. Consequently, exploration works best as atmosphere rather than as a particularly sophisticated open-world system.

Presentation is one of the game's biggest accomplishments. Character models successfully reproduce the recognizable anime aesthetic, while transformations, energy attacks, explosions, facial expressions, and cinematic sequences receive considerable attention. Major battles are especially impressive when elaborate animations and dramatic camera angles recreate iconic scenes. Voice performances and familiar sound effects further reinforce the sensation of playing through an animated Dragon Ball adventure. The visual presentation is not equally elaborate in every conversation or optional mission, but the most important moments receive enough attention to make them memorable.

Another important strength is the substantial amount of single-player content. This is primarily a story-driven RPG rather than a competitive fighting experience, so its appeal comes from developing characters and progressing through a lengthy adventure. Players who enjoy completing optional activities can spend considerable additional time pursuing side stories, collecting materials, improving Community Boards, developing abilities, hunting achievements, and strengthening characters beyond what is strictly required to finish the narrative.

Steam Deck compatibility is a notable advantage. The game is officially Steam Deck Verified, with its core functionality working through the handheld's controls and its interface remaining usable on the smaller display. Controller prompts and general navigation are appropriately supported, while the game can run using settings suitable for the device. Its viewpoint and methodical pacing also translate naturally to portable play, although demanding visual settings can still make sensible performance adjustments worthwhile for players prioritizing battery life or consistent performance.

The game's shortcomings mostly involve repetition. Standard encounters eventually become predictable, resource collection can feel excessive, and some RPG systems provide incremental statistical improvements rather than genuinely changing how the game is played. The open environments are also less sophisticated than those of dedicated open-world RPGs. However, these weaknesses are easier to accept when the game is approached as a Dragon Ball experience first and a conventional RPG second.

DRAGON BALL Z: KAKAROT ultimately succeeds by recognizing that the appeal of the series extends beyond enormous battles. It provides the expected transformations, energy clashes, villains, and destructive confrontations while also allowing players to fly around the world, train, eat, fish, explore, and spend time with familiar characters. Its RPG mechanics occasionally lack depth and its structure can become repetitive, but the combination of cinematic storytelling, accessible combat, extensive content, and affectionate treatment of the source material makes it an excellent choice for fans seeking a substantial single-player Dragon Ball adventure.

Rating: 9/10

At the beginning it appeared to be a phenomenal game, but as the hours went by, I started noticing it's only a mid title wrapped up in amazing visuals.[list]
[*]Single player JRPG with semi open world regions a'la Dragon Age Inquisition. I'm surprised this isn't another Budokai Tenkaichi clone. They actually wanted to create something different and I applaud them, even though the end result is full of open world tropes, e.g. endless collectibles, or meaningless side quests.
[*]Looks really frigging good. It's really hard to create convincing 2D anime characters in a 3D engine. Sometimes it makes them look really weird. Look at Xenoverse 2. In Kakarot they somehow made it work, though in bad lighting they still appear derpy. Not only that, but they added incredible details, e.g. Goku's Gi and hair have actual physics. Pre-rendered cutscenes are absolutely phenomenal.
[*]Combat appears to be similar to Budokai Tenkaichi, but it plays very differently against bosses. It plays more strategically. They have attacks you need to avoid, phases activated at specific health levels, including stuns, AoE with visible affected area indicators, and super powerful beams.
[*]Some quests flesh out the story better, e.g. Gohan's relationship with Android 16 which gives some insight on why he was so influential in his SSJ2 transformation. You also unlock a fair number of side quests post-game.
[*]Great attention to detail, e.g. the character icons are updating as the story progresses. I love the references and collectibles from the original Dragon Ball series.
[*]Community Boards are an interesting concept, though only two of those are worth the effort.
[*]QoL where, after getting all items needed for a side quest, you're automatically teleported to the quest giver. Manual saves.
[/list]
Unfortunately...
[list]
[*]In reality it's Dragon Ball Z: Son Gohan. Goku, aka Kakarot, is a side character in his own game. Yes, DBZ is more Gohan centric, but both in anime and manga Goku is present much more frequently than in this game. I guess Kakarot is more marketable, but this is bordering on false advertising.
[*]Bosses force you to think strategically, but combat mechanics themselves are fairly shallow and spammy; Xenoverse has more depth. I hope you enjoy all enemies having super armor on command 80% of the time. Solo battles against multiple opponents (i.e., all skill fights) are incredibly annoying as you're being tossed around like a ragdoll, trying to get your bearings, being forced to spam specific moves, preferably AoE ones. Particle effects of some blasts can literally obscure the entire screen making you blind to everything that is happening around you.
[*]Namek is disappointing, as it's just a single map in which you're being more or less railroaded with invisible walls.
[*]Almost shocking number of cutscenes, but it's to be expected as it follows the storyline very closely. All of them can be fast forwarded, thankfully. At the same time, some key moments are straight up missing, e.g. traversing Snake Way, training with Kaio, Vegeta's Final Flash against Perfect Cell, Goku giving Cell a Senzu Bean, or Gohan playing with Cell too much which was one of the major causes of Cell being able to blow himself up.
[*]All minigames are throwaway: racing (in a DB game?), fishing, baseball. All of these are here because someone, at some point in the series, performed those activities. You'll do them once, get the achievements, and then never touch them again.
[*]It's a JRPG with random encounters... but they're pointless. Grinding XP is not worth the effort, since all playable characters in the main story receive enough XP to catch up to the required level when their time comes. Farming orbs that are dropped by them is only worth it for the absurdly expensive DLC abilities of Goku and Vegeta.
[*]Loot is meaningless. All ore and car parts are for racing minigames nobody cares about. All food: apples, meat, apples, fish, apples, carrots, apples, rice. Have I mentioned apples yet?... You'll never eat food; at best you need it to complete side quests. There is no need for the buffs it provides with the exception of Beerus boss fights. Zeni? You'll use Zeni to upgrade the Gravity Room and maybe buy healing items, though those quickly become plentiful. That's it. D Medals and Z Orbs are the only noteworthy ones.[/list]

[list][*]DLC 1: A New Power Awakens Part 1 is just Goku and Vegeta being randomly teleported to Beerus' planet and trained. No story. There's only 2 side quests, the rest is essentially XP grind with new attacks and Super Saiyan God transformation.
[*]DLC 2: A New Power Awakens Part 2 has a short story, in addition to an even higher level cap, Super Saiyan Blue, a horde mode, and even more XP grinding. Level 300 Beerus fight is the true final boss fight of the game.
[*]DLC 3: Trunks - The Warrior of Hope is the first DLC worth a damn with a story 4-6 hours long. It not only covers the future version of Android/Cell Sagas, but also Majin Buu Saga, which was only briefly mentioned in Dragon Ball Super. It's sad, it's satisfying, it's epic. No wonder it's everyone's favorite DLC... because it's the best one.
[*]DLC 4: Bardock - Alone Against Fate. You can explore a small portion of planet Vegeta which, correct me if I'm wrong, is a first in DB video games. 4-5 hours long and doesn't go above and beyond like the previous DLC, with the exception of a short section with Kid Vegeta. Bardock's portrayal is that of the Bardock - Father of Goku TV special, instead of Dragon Ball Minus, or DBS Broly. It's a bit of a missed opportunity: no Great Ape combat, no King Vegeta, Gine, Raditz, Paragus, Broly. Nothing transfers to the main game. The negative reviews are not because the DLC is bad, but because it's only good, when it could have been amazing.
[*]DLC 5: 23rd World Tournament - started it, didn't finish, I was too tired of the game.
[*]DLC 6: Goku's Next Journey - starts with fight against Kid Buu, the same as in the base game. Then after the introduction, first thing you have to do is catch 3 fish. I quit.
[/list]

One and done. No replay value whatsoever. Feels like a prequel to a much better game. Enjoyable, but buy on sale.

Dragon Ball Z: Kakarot has the best campaign out of all the DBZ games and probably the best recreation of certain episodes/chapters from the anime/manga that have been made so far. But that doesn’t mean it is perfect.
Its combat is shallow. There isn’t really anything stopping you from just spamming your most powerful skills over and over again, which is often the best way to deal with enemies. The game only goes through the main sagas of DBZ and has got a very underwhelming prequel to Xenoverse 2 after the Buu Saga. The events of the original Dragon Ball were relegated to only mentions and other events such as those from movies or GT, which have already been covered by Budokai Tenkaichi 3, are not even mentioned at all as far as I am aware. (And events from Super are being treated as paid DLC.) The game is filled with mechanics that feel tacked on and while it did try to recreate smaller episodes as side quests, those side quests are unfortunately often very underwhelming.
But that aside, there is still a lot to enjoy from this game. And for as shallow as the “open world” and the mechanics tied to it are, it can still be fun to fly around the world of Dragon Ball. It is something that should definitely make any fan of the series happy.
Best Dragonball game i have ever played since the PS2 Budokai Tenkaichi trilogy. This is what we all have really waited for.

This game is a beautiful remastering of the full story of Dragonball Z, in videogame form. You can join Goku and his friends through his journey, from the dynamics beginnings of the Saiyan Saga, to the thrilling finish at the Buu Saga. Fully voice acted from the original Japanese and English VAs

This game truly allows you to FEEL like Goku and co., from driving like a maniac and destroying general riff-raff here and there, this game captures the essence of what it would truly feel like to be in the Dragonball Universe from the perspective of the characters.

Frankly, the best part of the game is how frequently it goes on sale, from full price to like 15 AUD, and I'd say thats worth it to live the experience that is Dragonball Z.

[h3] Dragon Ball Z Kakarot - Nostalgia on a plate! [/h3]

[b] Pros [/b]
- The story very closely follows the source material with minor cuts and changes likely due to time constraints. 
- Characters, although cartoony, look eerily similar to their anime counterparts. 
- Fishing, mining, foraging events are dotted on the map as an added activity. No huge open world game should go without as many of them as possible, as long as they enhance the core game, not diminish, hurry or force the player to do them. 
- Goku can go fishing with his ol' pals. They won't comment or sneakily throw stones at him when resting so that's a plus, at least. 
- Items, characters, events and references are explained in the Z Encyclopedia. Whoever worked on this should know that Gohan the scholar would be proud. 
- Memorial spots will convince our main character to relay his feelings on events from the original DB. Quite the trip down memory lane!
- The developers made sure to add short breaks in the storyline for the player to be able to manage their team, including skills, inventory, community boards, etc. 
- Permanent food buffs apply to all characters so don't hold back on full course meals!
- Mass Effect 1 had planetary exploration with the Mako, Spore had the creature and tribal stages and this game has underwater exploration. Neat!
- The DB wish system is a welcome addition and was worth pursuing during interludes.
- The fighting system is quite straighforward once you're familiarized with it. 
- The game is mostly stable, however I did encounter a few bugs/glitches and one UE5 crash when building a car. Moreover, I got two softlocks where the ESC and M key wouldn't register. Once that happens the game won't autosave either. Restarting fixes it but you lose a bit of progress. 

[b] Cons [/b]
- Changing the layout to keyboard + mouse at EVERY startup was mandatory for me, as the game does NOT in fact save this setting.
- The way the game menu works makes it clear the they had consoles in mind throughout development.
- Not all dialogue lines have been voice acted. Most, even long lines, have short interjection sounds added to them which is detrimental to immersion. 
- Autosave without multiple backup auto saves and no F5 quicksave.
- For food items there is no "cook all" or "eat all" option. You need to do one thing at a time. Pointless time waster, if you ask me.
- Relatively slow start-up time. The fastest I could get in-game was 51.2 seconds. This did not include switching the keyboard layout or checking for the last saved game.
- Guru's lip animations are funny and sad at the same time. 
- Power levels, at times, can be quite inaccurate. Krillin at lvl 22 had slightly more BP than Gohan at 28 (post Guru) or Piccolo with more BP than Goku right after Trunks showed up. 
- Activating powers from the skill tree sometimes fails and the action must be repeated.
- Support characters can get stuck sometimes while trying to get to you. Very minor issue, but the glitchy sound they make is amusing.

Dragon Ball Z: Kakarot: The Ultimate Interactive Tribute to Akira Toriyama
As a lifelong Dragon Ball fan who has played everything from Budokai to Xenoverse, I can say that DBZ: Kakarot is the definitive way to experience the Z-Saga. Having 100% completed the game and unlocked every achievement, I didn’t just play through the story; I lived in that world, and the journey was nothing short of legendary.

Living the Lore
While most DBZ games focus purely on the fights, Kakarot focuses on the life of a Z-Warrior.

The World: Flying over Mount Paozu, visiting Capsule Corp, or exploring a beautifully recreated Namek felt like stepping into the anime.

Sub-Stories: For a fan, the side quests are gold. They bridge gaps in the lore and bring back forgotten characters like Eighter (Android 8) or Launch, making the world feel cohesive and alive.

The Completionist’s Dream (and Grind)
Getting that 100% mark was a labor of love. Unlike other RPGs where the grind feels like a chore, Kakarot rewards your curiosity.

The Z-Encyclopedia: Filling this out was my favorite part. It’s a treasure trove of nostalgia that reminded me why I fell in love with this franchise in the first place.

Post-Game Content: Taking down the secret boss, Mira, and maxing out the Community Boards required a deep understanding of the game's RPG mechanics. It wasn't just about mashing buttons; it was about strategy, cooking the right meals, and optimizing your soul emblems.

Flashy, Impactful Combat
The combat system perfectly captures the scale of the show. Seeing the environment crumble during a massive Kamehameha or a Final Flash never gets old. While it’s accessible for newcomers, the late-game battles and the "Villainous" party encounters actually demand mastery of the dodge and surge mechanics, providing a satisfying challenge for those aiming for the Platinum.

The Verdict
Dragon Ball Z: Kakarot isn't just a fighting game; it’s an open-world love letter. It respects the source material down to the smallest detail. If you want to feel the weight of Goku’s sacrifice or the intensity of Gohan’s growth, this is the game that delivers it best.

Final Thought: To 100% this game is to truly honor the legacy of the Z-Fighters. It’s a long road from Raditz to Kid Buu, but every single second was worth it.

This game has a lot of nice things; the maps (except for all those ugly orbs littering the screen in every single moment, "damaging" the panoramas), many cutscenes (there are some 100x more epic than what they were in the anime, but there are also some that are 100x uglier, for some inexplicable reason), all the ways to improve characters... and there would be room to make them better and add more cool stuff (like actual training to raise stats), but let's say that all those things are perfect as is...
Yet, there is just ONE major issue in the whole game, and unfortunately it's in the core gameplay mechanic, which is combat: that issue is ALL enemies having super-armor on 80% of the time you're attacking them.

For those who don't know, super/hyper-armor is when you attack an opponent and they may (or may not, in some games) take actual damage to their health, BUT they won't feel the hits "physically", so to speak.
In other words, say you're hitting an enemy in the face repeatedly with a combo...well, you'll deal numeric damage, but your hits won't stagger the target as you'd expect, they won't interrupt their Ki charging or special moves, or anything like that... basically, you hit them, but at the same time they're completely free to hit you, as if you were doing nothing to them.
Sometimes they even rush straight into one of your ultra powerful Ki attack beams, attack you, and even interrupt your attack by doing that.
That's it. ALL, and I really mean ALL enemies, even the most insignificant one, have that, in this game. They have this super-armor on most of the time, while you never have it, so you can't fight them the way you'd expect (especially if you played Dragon Ball Tenkaichi Budokai and those sort of games that had actually enjoyable fighting mechanics, and expected this game was the same, from the videos you watched).

Enemies getting super-armor every few seconds, even in the middle of being attacked, makes you not understand what's happening (basically, if you're hitting them "properly" or if you're hitting them while they have super-armor), and you constantly get interrupted by even the smallest hit, while you can throw at them nuclear bombs on the face without interrupting their attacks.

There are ways to cheese this, for example just keeping your distance dodging everything, and blasting the enemy in the moment that you'll learn it stands still with no super-armor (not counting that some story fights even have scripted moments where the enemy will just make their special move regardless, interrupting anything you're doing to them), but this makes fights all the same tedious chore, rather than epic battles.

Basically, instead of programming a decent AI and good mechanics, the developers just gave ridiculous amounts of super-armor to all enemies to make them somehow challenging.
This is bad, bad, BAD game design. It's not even the only issue with combat, but really, if they fixed this one and made combat good, the game could easily jump from a 5 to a 9.
Unfortunatley, two years from publishng as we are at this moment, it's very unlikely that there will ever be such a big revamp of combat, and this game will probably remain an embarrassing missed opportunity for a timeless gem.

The only thing that can keep you playing this after you witness the super-armor madness with your eyes, again and again, is the mere love for Dragon Ball.
If it wasn't Dragon Ball (or something else you love) and was just an original IP without particularly compelling plots and characters, you'd probably drop a game like this very soon. It's really a shame.

Dragon Ball Z: Kakarot. A game developed by CyberConnect2 and published by Bandai Namco.

I am a anime fan at heart, From the childhood classics such as the original Dragon ball, Digimon, Pokemon and Evangelion to the much more recent Death Note and Code Geass. So Dragon Ball Z has always been a staple of my anime collection and intake. The story is long and intense, the characters are love-able and the world is amazing filled with history and memories.
So when i see that a new Dragon Ball game is on the horizon i get extremely excited at the prospect that this one might scratch all the Dragon Ball itches i have without having to slog through the 9 seasons of the anime series.
Dragon Ball Z: Kakarot or DBZK as i'll refer to it on going was a great attempt at it. More of which i'll touch on below.

I break my reviews down into 4 categories, Story, Gameplay, Visuals and Audio. Followed by a conclusive section that sums up the review. If you aren't partial to long reviews feel free to scroll to the bottom,
Lets get started.

Story: 8/10
I wanted to rate the story higher, but its just more classic Dragon Ball Z with a lot of insignificant filler placed between the sagas, From fighting Vegeta in the Saiyan Saga all the way through to the encounter with Buu this is your base line story for any Dragon Ball Z game. The filler on the other hand doesn't really affect much in terms of the world or history, feels like just content for the sake of content and maybe even a small nostalgia trip. There's not a lot to go on here, because you either love the Dragon Ball Z saga or you don't and if you do, you know the story already. The side stories are intriguing enough to keep you occupied but the writing feels lazy and a little sloppy at times, and the subtitles often differ greatly from what has actually been said.

Gameplay: 6/10
This was a hard one. Masquerading as a RPG, Open World Fighting game. It attempts all of these without really doing any of them well. Let me explain.
RPG, It is an RPG at it's base line, but the real expectation of an RPG is to experience a levelling system, gain experience, invest that experience into skills and build the character the way you want to. There's no real way to do that in a game like this, Goku is as powerful as Goku is, as are the remaining roster characters. They attempted it here vaguely by giving you the illusion of free choice, but its ultimately futile in the long run as grinding for experience is useless, levelling your characters is a formality and the skill tree is tacky and makes little sense in the story of the game.
Open World, It's as open world as you can get from a Dragon Ball game, the map is broken down into "zones" that are fairly sizeable in their own right, but far from an "Open World".
Fighting, This is probably one of the worst fighting game experiences I've witnessed, The boss sequences are more of a classic Metroid style boss fight where you avoid the attack, and counter attack at an opening. There is no finesse to the situations, no deflections, no interruptions and no real way to cancel out of your combos once started. I was horrendously disappointed with the combat in this game because the videos made it look so amazing and it followed so closely behind Xenoverse and FighterZ which both developed combat in a really intuitive way.
I have been picking on this game quite a lot, which is harsh because the overall experience is enjoyable, if not a little tedious at times, as there isn't a lot of diversity in enemy, as in (not including boss fights) maybe 5 or 6 enemy variations total, and they end up quite lengthy for very little reward which can be extremely exhaustive when you just want to fly around and do the side quests and keep getting hindered by weak but long fights that are more of a time consumption than a challenge.
The side quest system though as a whole is enjoyable and offers a rather diverse range of activities that should keep you busy for a long while, from hunting down the dragon balls to helping random characters from the series.
I have also found quite a few spelling and grammatical errors in the subtitles of the game, not a glaring issue but it really shows the game is lacking polish.
It does quite a few things well though in both theory and practicality, The map system is tight and easy to understand, as well as a system called the "Community Boards" which let you link certain characters to an aspect of your adventure, increasing your income, or your overall battle strength depending on your choices. Not a bad effort overall really considering the history of anime games. Definitely a step in the right direction in my honest opinion.

Visual: 6/10
It's an anime in game format. Quite beautiful in its own right, but it's not redefining anything, or even improving upon its past incarnations in any notable way. The game runs flawlessly at ultra settings on a mid to high end PC, never dropping at all below 60fps. There are however quite a few graphical flaws that hinder the experience, characters slowly floating away during cinematics and tearing as you flight around, even some occasions of un-rendered and disjointed landscapes.

Audio: 9/10
This is probably the best part of DBZK. The audio is tremendous and anyone who is an avid fan of the series will appreciate the effort drawn here. The original voice acting cast are back and flawlessly knit into the world. It's at times completely like you are watching the anime again. The music is nostalgic and subtle and doesn't draw attention away from the experience but helps elevate it significantly. A wonderful audio experience that was just a beautifully orchestrated nostalgic trip.

Story: 8/10
Gameplay: 6/10
Visual: 6/10
Audio: 9/10
Conclusion: 7/10

Overall: 
Classic Dragon Ball Z through and through. Lacking quite a lot of polish in some areas and feeling a little hollow and exhausting at times. However, the base experience is still astounding and offers quite a lot of enjoyment that will keep you occupied happily for several hours. Probably not the best Dragon Ball game out there, but definitely a step in the right direction and i'm looking forward to seeing where this will lead it. But if you are after a fresh Dragon Ball Z experience this isn't where you'll find it. Recommended out of nostalgia and enjoyment from a world and story i adore, but not a lot of it is outstanding as a whole. 

Worth a buy, but not at full price. I'd also suggest waiting to see what the season pass will entail before going headlong into it.

One of the most beloved franchises in anime, bogged down by repetitive and rushed gameplay. The Dragon Ball franchise is one of my most favorite series, so the games are obviously very critical to me in their execution. Bandai brings elements from their previous entries and tries something new with an open world feature. Fly across the DB world and explore the regions within. The idea is an amazing image of the world, but it has many flaws that hurt the spirit of many fans. To start, what makes this game feel rushed is the fact that a good portion of the story is either told in a mediocre cut scene or just completely skipped entirely. A mediocre cutscene would be such as Goku coming back from yardrat and him explaining where he has been, only for the game to cut to a black screen and come back with the story told “behind” the scenes. This is heavy throughout the game. Yes, we all know the story and it has been told thousands of times, but that doesn’t stop the fans from buying the next title. And Bandai knows that. Many game companies push out half assed games these days and still gamers buy them, myself included. In my opinion, the last great DBZ game to bless us gamers was Budokai Tenkaichi 3. The roster and gameplay coupled with the environment were top notch.

Everyone loves free things. This is what the dragon balls are for right? Well yes, you get free things in the game. And you really don’t have to work hard at all to find them. YEP! The map shows you exactly where they are. The dragon balls are on a real world timer based off the last time you summoned Shenron. Once they reappear, you get a notification and the map shows which region and the radar shows you the exact location via an icon on the mini map. You could easily grind your way through the game via the dragon balls. But what fun is that really? The rewards all actually not all that worth it. The dragon balls should have been a little harder to find and actually require you to use the radar to find them. 

This game brings you few playable characters, NPC support characters, and everything else is minor.The environment is not destructible, and the rank up system is brought to you by a means of HEAVY grinding for different color orbs scattered throughout the map that barely give enough points to gain a new skill. The repetitive nature of going back and forth between maps to gather orbs, and fight off enemies in the sky, just make it really boring and really frustrating. There is so much lost potential as with this type of game, you could have told Dragon Ball, Dragon Ball Z, Dragon Ball GT, Dragon Ball Super, and all the movies to make 1 epic title, even if they were released as DLC.

A good thing going for the game would definitely have to be the difficulty scaling. Enemies 10 levels higher then you can and will waste your time. You will hardly do damage and will probably give up before you actually kill them. This forces you to gain more experience and skills before fighting them. But then also falls back on the repetitive grind. Surprisingly though, the game is quite stable for its size, and I did not encounter any bugs or glitches.

This game can truly become amazing if only it were polished more and more features added. As we all know, there will most likely be another DBZ game released in the future, but hopefully we get one that tells it all. That can blow the fans minds in its flesh out story and battles. Epic moves and fights, warping the ground and buildings. Tearing of the clothes and battle scars. Really does make me miss Tenkaichi 3.


All in all, this is a decent game to the franchise despite its flaws. I’m just a fan picking apart his favorite team. Pick it up for the story and nostalgia. To any true DBZ die hard fan, get this game on discount, it will disappoint you a little unfortunately. 

Some things I’d like to see in the future on titles or this game:
Redo the story and actually make it fleshed out and/or tell the story from the very beginning
Fix Voice sync
Bring the PLAYABLE roster of the likes of FighterZ or Tenkaichi 3
(For the PvP oriented) Bring multiplayer
Add a seperate mode to actually fight against AI like in the older games
Bring world tournament to acquire optional things (tie in cosmetics instead of a cash shop)
Go back to the first DBZ game and start from there in pulling elements from all the previous entries

Hoo boy, the idiot patrol is out in full force for this one so let's clear some things up:

Dragonball Z: Kakarot, like most PC ports, may not work out of the box. Thankfully getting it to work is an easy fix.
 - For those experiencing crashes: Update everything, all of your drivers, and make sure your game is version 1.03. There were several day one patches to make the game more stable and compatible.
 - For those using Mouse and Keyboard, or even PS4 controllers, as opposed to Xbox: Yes, the game does support it, but you have to go into the menu and enable the button prompts yourself. For PS4 Controllers this would be "Type A", for Mouse and Keyboard it would be "Mouse + Keyboard."
 - For those of you suffering from fps locks. Turn vsync off in-game. Yes this does create screen tear, but there's a fix for that.
 - For those experiencing screen tear: Turn the display mode to "Borderless Windowed Mode." Don't ask me, it just works.

Voila, by not being lazy, you've fixed all the problems that people are bashing the game for.

(4½ stars if half-stars were possible - even with its flaws, this is one of the best DBZ games around)

============

Review:

I'm not a hardcore fan of DBZ, but I have watched the anime - and this game is fairly faithful to the anime (it does skip some stuff and fast forward many things, but it works).

When I bought this game, I was expecting a fighting game with a little other stuff on the side - and I was really surprised.

It's not a fighting game - it's more like an open world RPG in the world of DBZ. Characters have levels and skill trees, and there's quests, items, crafting and stuff.

It sort of gives me Yakuza vibes, like the main story is great and all but it has all kinds of extra stuff for you to do as well. Though it also suffers from the same problem as Yakuza 0 - the side quests aren't voice acted.

It has all the typical things you'd expect from a DBZ game - you get to fly around the world at supersonic speeds, there's transformations, speedy fighting and energy attacks.

The game has captured the feeling of speed really well - if you just jog around it's slow, but if you RUN across the land it feels really fast.. and if you fly, it's so fast that you'll have trouble controlling the movement until you get used to it.

Graphics look nice and they're faithful to the anime. The world looks colorful and vibrant, and it's pleasant to look at. 

Sounds are also faithful to the anime, but imo the music is not good, other than the legendary intro song.

You can choose between japanese and english voice actors, so why can't you choose between japanese and english music? Maybe some legal issues.. but I grew up with the Bruce Faulconer versions so it pisses me off a bit. Vegeta turning into a super saiyan without the piano of doom just feels wrong to me.

============

Controls take a moment to learn, but after that they feel quite natural. It's like the first times you're flying around, it's clunky.. but you learn and it becomes smooth and then you just fly from one location to the next in one perfect motion.

Combat is quite simple and I really like it that way. It's in a 3rd-person view, and you're locked into an enemy always. There's no difficult inputs to do, and it's really simple to pull off combos. The simplicity makes 1-on-1 fights pretty much the same always, same combos work against different enemies - though different characters have different moves, so it's not EXACTLY the same always and you need to adjust your style. But there can be multiple enemies at once in a fight, which breaks the pattern.

Regular enemies of the game are just boring. And unnecessary, they could be removed and just allow players to train with other characters to get xp. In my opinion they are annoying, useless speed bumps.

The villanous versions are fine, since you don't have to hunt down too many of them, and they show up on the map.

============

Overall, I think DBZ: Kakarot is an excellent game. I can recommend it even to people who haven't watched the anime - though of course it is more appealing for people who have done so.

If you could choose between the current music and the Bruce Faulconer versions, and if they removed the boring regular enemies, it would easily be a five-star game in my eyes.

But even like this, it's an excellent game and I recommend you to buy it, if you like DBZ or just any open world RPGs.

============

+ Feeling of speed is very well done
+ Simple but fun combat
+ Massive amounts of stuff to do

The Bad 👎
- No Bruce Faulconer music!
- Boring regular enemies
- Side-quests are not voice acted

Having experienced this game as I have and watched the show up to the end of super I think I can give you a fair assessment of the quality of this game.

Whilst the attention to detail can be quite apparent I felt the game borders on the edge on what I consider "good enough to distract you" but lacks some quality control in some areas. I do enjoy the game tries to fill in the gaps of time between what the characters were doing beyond what the show presents us - that's actually a good quality I didn't expect to see and most of the game's is littered with what are called "memories" that are short bursts of information portraying the original dragon ball content to remind us of Goku's origins.

While an extra eye of detail can be commended unfortunately some of the time spent on that could have gone into improving the combat: often I felt the controls are stiff - using a keyboard just doesn't feel right due to how fast your need to use your fingers to be pull off combos. But that being said, most "combat" ends up with you holding down power, spamming the specials over and over and then repeating the same tired attack, charge use special combination because the ai doesn't know how to challenge the player besides exclaiming what they are about to do while a giant red laser warns players they're about to attack - the health in this game requires you to mundanely collect resources from the map to gain zeni: with the only alternative to use the dragonballs to give you money that isn't that great of a wish when you consider most quests grant you things that you can sell anyway.

I think the game lacks polish in what you can buy, how the upgrades should work and how the game should play out. If it was my design I would have removed the skill tree "abilities" to upgrade only after you had progressed - the selection of skills should have been limited to just the upgraded forms of the attacks and removed the inferior version as most ki costs are the same - redundancy is something programmers should be avoiding.

The combat needed more to it, I felt unchallenged, it felt too on rails and there were no exciting moments other than the occasional cool new move thrown in there the lackluster progression of combat holds this game back.

I do like how this game plays for the lore reasons, but I only wish the game played more like other combat titles which had more flexible controls, better "counters" and the AI would present you with a challenge that wasn't just "spam" health items and "spam" specials and win. The combat is otherwise too slow and clunky for me to even consider this fun. If you're playing this: have an open mind, don't go in with the concept of expecting good fighting, instead enjoy the plotlines - you'll find most of the content cannot really be enjoyed until you do most of the missions themselves: I find this is to purposely make players replay the game and go back to finish off the content they missed. Fortunately you have a time machine to do most of that later on.

To summarise:
- Combat could be better improved.
- Travel is slow and some mundane elements could be shortened to make the game seem less of a chore to get through.
- Maps are overly sized: most of it is just space with nothing in it: while I enjoy the exploration aspects, the lack of content in this aspect is very apparent.
- The Memories seem rather pointless as only hardcore fans of the show would understand the plot-points from the original Dragon ball episodes (not Z).
- The game shines in the story telling elements: but only because it has the content to refer to - so as much as I praise the story, most of this can just be attributed to the fact the game is just regurgitating the same story from the show. I get the impression they really wanted to make their own story in the game but couldn't due to having to stick to the plot from the show: if this was the case, maybe you could have just made the scenes of fighting the main villians short missions rather than make the game revolve around them.

-Most of this game could be summed up as: Have you seen the show? Oh well it's that, but longer and you have to recollect the dragon balls every time you want to fight people you already killed - to fill up your community board: wasn't all that work worth it though? (inner screaming) it's repetitive and the only direction it can go is telling you the plot of DBZ: I feel this game is better suited to those that haven't seen the show and even then I'd still would prefer they watch the series instead rather than have their impression be ruined by bad mechanics in a video game.

I do hope that the later DLC makes up for it's lame repetitive state - I don't plan on buying Goku's dad DLC as it's 15 quid for the opportunity to basically sit there and gawk at a lemming: why would I pay for that? I'm glad I just stuck to paying for the Season pass as I didn't realise just how bad the game felt until halfway through the content. The game feels like it's content has been stretched and not for the right reasons.

I'd advise anyone who is just looking at what content to get in terms of the DLC to stick with the first season pass - the second season pass only offers you promise of content that doesn't exist right now, which is not worth your purchase unless you are willing to wait.

Dragon Ball Z: Kakarot is either the best Dragon Ball Z game ever or slightly behind "The Legend of Goku" series on GBA. Being able to relive all of the Z series and some of Dragon Ball Super through DLC is already a great/fun time but add in fun combat with heavy RPG elements and I am all in.

If you are worried that you aren't good at fighting games or dislike them - don't worry because I am not a massive fan either. But Dragon Ball Z: Kakarot finds a good balance of challenge with ways to make it easier. Bringing in combat similar to Budakai along with ways to buff your character through meals or simply over-level yourself before a big story battle, there are plenty of ways to make this "fighting" game easier. But if you want a challenge, that is there as well and something you can do by avoiding a lot of the side content until the end game when experience doesn't matter as much.

Whether you are a veteran of the series, fighting games, or simply just interested in this game - I honestly would recommend this to all for a great experience.
